:::{#def-matrix-induced-inner-product}
#### Matrix-induced inner product ($\matr{A}$-inner product)

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ symmetric positive definite matrix (@def-positive-definite)
($\matr{A} = \tp{\matr{A}}$ and $\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx > 0$ for all nonzero $\vx \in \reals^p$).
The **matrix-induced inner product** (or **$\matr{A}$-inner product**)
on $\reals^p$ is defined for all $\vx, \vy \in \reals^p$ by

$$
\iprod{\vx}{\vy}_{\matr{A}} \eqdef \tp{\vx} \matr{A} \vy.
$$

The space $\reals^p$ equipped with $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}}$
is an inner product space (@def-inner-product-space).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-matrix-induced-inner-product}
#### Properties of the matrix-induced inner product

For every $p \times p$ symmetric positive definite matrix $\matr{A}$,
the function $\iprod{\vx}{\vy}_{\matr{A}} = \tp{\vx} \matr{A} \vy$ satisfies the four inner product axioms (@def-inner-product):
positivity, definiteness, linearity in the first slot, and symmetry.
Thus $(\reals^p, \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}})$ is an inner product space (@def-inner-product-space).

Taking $\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p$ recovers the standard dot product (@exm-dot-product-inner-product),
while taking $\matr{A} = \operatorname{diag}(c_1, \ldots, c_p)$ recovers the weighted inner product (@exm-weighted-inner-product).

Conversely, every inner product on $\reals^p$ has this form for a unique symmetric positive definite matrix $\matr{A}$, whose $(i, j)$ entry is $A_{ij} = \iprod{\vecf{e}_i}{\vecf{e}_j}$, where $\vecf{e}_1, \ldots, \vecf{e}_p$ are the standard basis vectors (@def-indicator-vector).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

- **positivity**: $\iprod{\vx}{\vx}_{\matr{A}} = \tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx \ge 0$ for all $\vx \in \reals^p$,
  because $\matr{A}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite);
- **definiteness**: $\iprod{\vx}{\vx}_{\matr{A}} = 0$ if and only if $\vx = \vzero_{p \times 1}$,
  by definition of a positive definite matrix (@def-positive-definite);
- **linearity in the first slot**: for all $\vx, \vy, \vecf{z} \in \reals^p$ and real numbers $a, b$,
  $$
  \ba
  \iprod{a\,\vx + b\,\vy}{\vecf{z}}_{\matr{A}}
  &= \tp{(a\,\vx + b\,\vy)}\,\matr{A}\vecf{z}
  && \text{(definition of } \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}} \text{)}
  \\
  &= (a\,\tp{\vx} + b\,\tp{\vy})\,\matr{A}\vecf{z}
  && \text{(@thm-transpose-sum, @def-scalar-mult, @def-matrix-transpose)}
  \\
  &= a\,\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vecf{z} + b\,\tp{\vy}\matr{A}\vecf{z}
  && \text{(@thm-matmul-distrib)}
  \\
  &= a\,\iprod{\vx}{\vecf{z}}_{\matr{A}} + b\,\iprod{\vy}{\vecf{z}}_{\matr{A}}
  && \text{(definition of } \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}} \text{)}
  \ea
  $$
- **symmetry**: because $\tp{\vy}\matr{A}\vx$ is a $1 \times 1$ scalar and $\matr{A}$ is symmetric ($\tp{\matr{A}} = \matr{A}$),
  $$
  \ba
  \iprod{\vy}{\vx}_{\matr{A}}
  &= \tp{\vy}\matr{A}\vx
  && \text{(definition of } \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}} \text{)}
  \\
  &= \tp{\paren{\tp{\vy}\matr{A}\vx}}
  && \text{(a scalar equals its transpose)}
  \\
  &= \tp{\vx}\tp{\matr{A}}\vy
  && \text{(@thm-transpose-product, twice)}
  \\
  &= \tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vy
  && \text{($\matr{A}$ is symmetric)}
  \\
  &= \iprod{\vx}{\vy}_{\matr{A}}
  && \text{(definition of } \iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\matr{A}} \text{)}
  \ea
  $$

{{< slidebreak >}}

For the converse, let $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}$ be any inner product on $\reals^p$.
Any vectors $\vx, \vy \in \reals^p$ can be written in the standard basis as
$\vx = \sum_{i=1}^p x_i\,\vecf{e}_i$ and $\vy = \sum_{j=1}^p y_j\,\vecf{e}_j$ (@def-basis, @def-indicator-vector).
By linearity in both slots (@rem-inner-product-other-sources):

$$
\ba
\iprod{\vx}{\vy}
&= \iprod{\sum_{i=1}^p x_i\,\vecf{e}_i}{\sum_{j=1}^p y_j\,\vecf{e}_j}
&& \text{(expand in the standard basis)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^p \sum_{j=1}^p x_i y_j\,\iprod{\vecf{e}_i}{\vecf{e}_j}
&& \text{(linearity in both slots)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^p x_i \sum_{j=1}^p A_{ij} y_j
&& \text{(define } A_{ij} \eqdef \iprod{\vecf{e}_i}{\vecf{e}_j} \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{\vx} \matr{A} \vy.
&& \text{(@def-matvec-mult)}
\ea
$$

Symmetry of $\iprod{\cdot}{\cdot}$ ensures $A_{ji} = \iprod{\vecf{e}_j}{\vecf{e}_i} = \iprod{\vecf{e}_i}{\vecf{e}_j} = A_{ij}$,
so $\matr{A}$ is symmetric (@def-symmetric-matrix).
For any $\vx \neq \vzero$, $\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx = \iprod{\vx}{\vx} > 0$ by positivity and definiteness of the inner product,
so $\matr{A}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite).

For uniqueness, if another matrix $\matr{B}$ satisfies $\iprod{\vx}{\vy} = \tp{\vx}\matr{B}\vy$ for all $\vx, \vy$,
evaluating at $\vx = \vecf{e}_i$ and $\vy = \vecf{e}_j$ gives
$B_{ij} = \tp{\vecf{e}_i}\matr{B}\vecf{e}_j = \iprod{\vecf{e}_i}{\vecf{e}_j} = A_{ij}$,
so $\matr{B} = \matr{A}$.

:::
